direct_answer: In Northern Ireland, free support includes the Arthritis UK helpline (0800 5200 520), the NRAS helpline for rheumatoid arthritis, peer and online groups, Age NI, and your Health and Social Care Trust, which arranges community care, occupational therapy, equipment and falls services. Your GP can refer you.

content:
If you live in Northern Ireland with arthritis, including if you are older or becoming frail, there is free help available from charities, peer groups and health and social care services. This guide brings the main options together.

Services change, so check current details before you travel or rely on a group. This is educational information, not personal medical advice.

Helplines and charities

  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) runs a free helpline on 0800 5200 520, Monday to Friday, 9am to 6pm, and an online community. Its advisors are not medically trained, so they cannot give individual medical advice.
  • NRAS (National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society) offers information and support for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Age NI offers advice and services for older people, including on benefits, care and staying independent.

Health and Social Care Trusts

In Northern Ireland, health and social care are joined up and delivered by five Health and Social Care Trusts. Your Trust can provide:

  • An assessment of your care and support needs.
  • Community occupational therapy and equipment, such as grab rails and bathing aids.
  • Physiotherapy and falls prevention services.
  • Help at home and short breaks for carers.

Your GP can refer you, or you can contact your Trust directly.

Adapting your home

The Disabled Facilities Grant in Northern Ireland can pay up to £25,000 towards adaptations, depending on your income. It is usually arranged through the Housing Executive after an occupational therapy assessment.

Peer support

Support groups and online communities can reduce isolation and help with practical tips. Choose groups that are supportive and do not push unproven cures. Ask your GP practice about local groups and social prescribing, or check with your Trust or library.

Money and benefits

Advice NI and Citizens Advice can help with benefits, such as Attendance Allowance or Personal Independence Payment, and with housing questions.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Do I need a referral to join a support group?

Usually not. Most groups and helplines can be contacted directly.

Who arranges care at home in Northern Ireland?

Your Health and Social Care Trust. Contact your GP or the Trust to ask for an assessment.

Is there a frailty service where I live?

Services vary between Trusts. Ask your GP what is available locally.

If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
